multiScaleAC

Bivariate Moran’s I as a function of Gaussian kernel bandwidth: a functional curve I(h) over spatial scales, rather than a single value at one arbitrarily chosen scale.

Intended for ligand–receptor interaction analysis in spatial transcriptomics. Weights come directly from the kernel, row standardised, with no minimum weight threshold, so no cells or spots are dropped from the weight matrix. That is the main methodological difference from approaches that filter low kernel density estimates before computing the statistic.

The package name and the repository name differ, deliberately. The R package is multiScaleAC, matching the companion manuscript. The repository stays KernelCommunication, because that is the URL printed in the paper. Both are correct in their own scope.

Installation 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("ACSoupir/KernelCommunication")

Requires a C++ toolchain (Rcpp, RcppEigen). OpenMP is used when available; builds without it, including stock Apple clang, work single-threaded.

Quick start 

library(multiScaleAC)
data(ccRCCExample)

coords <- as.matrix(ccRCCExample[, c("x", "y")])

# Bandwidths are in COORDINATE UNITS. This dataset is in millimetres, so these
# come back in millimetres. Do not guess -- ask.
h <- suggest_bandwidths(coords, n_bandwidths = 8)

# Sanity-check before interpreting anything. `saturation` near 1 means the kernel
# is effectively a constant matrix and no result at that bandwidth is meaningful.
qc_neighborhoods(coords, h)

res <- multiScaleAC(
  coords, ccRCCExample$CD274, ccRCCExample$PDCD1,
  h = h, perms = 999
)
res <- compute_significance(res)

summary(res)
plot(res)

# Whole-curve significance in one number, needing no multiplicity correction
res@sup_p_value

The thing that goes wrong most often

Bandwidths are in the units of your coordinates. Get the scale wrong and the output is meaningless in a way that looks like a real answer.

ccRCCExample spans about 1.02 mm, with a median nearest-neighbour distance of 0.0073 mm:

qc_neighborhoods(coords, h = c(0.02, 25))
#>       h mean_neighbors  ...  saturation
#> 1  0.02          20.31  ...      0.0029
#> 2 25.00        7119.29  ...      0.9996

At h = 25 every pairwise weight is ≥ 0.9999 and each cell is effectively everyone’s neighbour. The kernel is constant, so I(h) collapses toward zero for every gene pair — about 2e-06 here, against 5e-02 at a sensible bandwidth. Earlier validation in this repository ran entirely inside that regime and reported agreement to 1e-18, which is agreement on an arithmetic identity rather than evidence of anything.

The manuscript’s range of 10–250 is in micrometres, i.e. 0.01–0.25 here. Use suggest_bandwidths(), then check qc_neighborhoods().

Inference

Two routes, both available on the same result.

Permutations (the default). Only the second gene is permuted. alternative defaults to "greater", the manuscript’s one-tailed upper test; "less" and a genuine "two.sided" are available.

Exact analytical moments. Because the weight matrix is row standardised and both genes are z-scored, the statistic is a linear permutation statistic, so the first four moments of its null and the full cross-bandwidth covariance have closed forms. They cost O(N) per bandwidth and are computed by default.

# No permutations at all
res <- multiScaleAC(coords, g1, g2, h = h, permute = "none")
res <- compute_significance(res, method = "moment")

# Or permute only where the diagnostics say an approximation cannot be trusted
res <- multiScaleAC(coords, g1, g2, h = h, perms = 999, permute = "flagged")
res <- compute_significance(res, method = "auto")
res@p_method   # records which method produced each p-value

What this buys is resolution, not speed. With 999 permutations the smallest reportable p-value is 1/1000, so p = 0.001 and p = 1e-6 are indistinguishable, and resolving 1e-5 needs roughly 100,000 permutations. The moments give it for free, and they are correct there: they agree with a 499,999-permutation run to under 1%. For a single gene pair the kernel sweep dominates, so dropping permutations saves about 1.7× on memory and only ~10% of wall clock.

Do not run pnorm() on the z_scores slot. It is an effect size. The permutation null is skewed whenever the expression data is, and on this package’s own example data a normal approximation is 100× anti-conservative in the tail — the direction that manufactures false positives. The measurements, and the reasoning behind the default approximation, are in inst/validation/results/README.md.

Downstream: functional data analysis

Each gene pair yields a curve, which is what makes functional data analysis natural. export_mxfda() produces a table for mxfda::add_summary_function(), as the manuscript uses for FPCA. Note that the bandwidth occupies mxfda’s radius column; ?export_mxfda explains why those are not the same quantity.

Many samples 

fovs <- split(ccRCCExample, ccRCCExample$fov)
results <- multiScaleAC_batch(
  fovs, h_vec = h, perms = 999,
  n_cores = 4, checkpoint_dir = "ckpt"    # resumable
)
plot_batch_comparison(results)

The manuscript applies FDR across gene pairs. To reproduce that, collect one p-value per pair — sup_p_value is the natural choice — and correct across the collection. adjust_pvalues() corrects across bandwidths within one result, which are strongly dependent and rarely what you want.

Reference implementation

soupir_moran_multi() is the reference implementation. It is permanently supported, is not deprecated, and is the oracle the test suite is pinned to: every fixture is generated from it, and a test detects any edit to it.
